sections.title: Implement Endpoint Security
sections.content:
CORE CONCEPT: DEVICE HARDENING
Hardening = changing configurations to secure systems by reducing vulnerabilities from default configs. Must be balanced against usability/functionality.
Principle of Least Functionality — a system should run only the protocols/services required by legitimate users, nothing more.
ENDPOINT HARDENING BASICS
• Interfaces — disable unused wired/wireless/modem/management interfaces explicitly (don't just leave unused)
• Services — disable unused services (local + remote-supporting)
• Application service ports — disable/block at firewall if not needed; watch for nonstandard ports (e.g., HTTP on 8080)
• Persistent storage — encrypt (disk encryption / self-encrypting drives)
BASELINE CONFIGURATION
• Configuration baseline — standard guideline/checklist for secure device config, often applied via template
• Baseline deviation reporting — testing actual config against the baseline template
• MBSA (Microsoft Baseline Security Analyzer) — legacy tool, replaced by Security Compliance Toolkit
• Windows: config stored in registry; GPOs (Group Policy Objects) push settings to registry at boot
ENDPOINT PROTECTION CONCEPTS
Term | Definition
Segmentation | Dividing network into subnets/segments with distinct controls, limiting lateral spread
Isolation | Restricting an individual device's network interaction to prevent lateral threat spread
Antivirus (A-V) | Signature-based detection; modern versions cover viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, PUPs, cryptojackers
Full Disk Encryption (FDE) | Encrypts entire drive contents; key usually stored in TPM (Trusted Platform Module); e.g., BitLocker
Self-Encrypting Drive (SED) | Drive controller performs crypto ops (not OS); uses DEK/MEK encrypted by an Authentication Key (AK)/Key Encryption Key (KEK); follows Opal Storage Specification
PATCH MANAGEMENT
• Vulnerability scanners find missing patches
• Auto-update: Windows Update; Linux via yum-cron or apt unattended-upgrades
• Enterprise: use patch management suites (e.g., SCCM/Endpoint Manager)
• Test patches before production deployment
• SolarWinds hack — example of a compromised update repository spreading malware
ADVANCED ENDPOINT PROTECTION
Acronym | Meaning
EDR | Endpoint Detection and Response — real-time/historical visibility, contains malware on a host, aids remediation
XDR | Extended Detection and Response — expands EDR scope to network, cloud, email, firewall data
MDR | Managed Detection and Response — hosted/outsourced security service class
HIDS | Host-based Intrusion Detection System — detects and alerts on suspicious activity
HIPS | Host-based Intrusion Prevention System — detects and actively blocks/mitigates threats
FIM | File Integrity Monitoring — verifies system files match authorized versions (e.g., Windows SFC, Tripwire, OSSEC)
UBA/UEBA | User (and Entity) Behavior Analytics — baselines normal behavior, alerts on anomalies (insider threats, compromised accounts)
ENDPOINT BREACH MITIGATION VECTORS
When endpoint security is breached, consider:
• Social Engineering — user-executed malware → security awareness training, review privilege level
• Vulnerabilities — software fault exploited → patch or isolate
• Lack of Security Controls — missing A-V/firewall/DLP/MDM → deploy or isolate
• Configuration Drift — undocumented changes (shadow IT) → reapply baseline
• Weak Configuration — baseline applied but insufficient → revise template
ACCESS CONTROL
• Access Control (general) — regulating permissions for users/software/systems to resources
• Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) — minimum permissions necessary, nothing more; supported by:
• Auditing user roles/privileges
• Removing unused accounts
• Temporary/just-in-time privileges
• RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) — permissions tied to predefined roles
• ACL (Access Control List) — rules specifying allow/deny for users/groups on resources (routers, firewalls, file systems)
• ACE (Access Control Entry) — individual entry within an ACL (user/group + permissions)
Linux File Permissions:
• r (read) = 4, w (write) = 2, x (execute) = 1
• Contexts: owner (u), group (g), others (o)
• Example: chmod 755 home = owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x
• Symbolic mode example: chmod g+w,o-x home
EXECUTION CONTROL
• Allow list (approved list) — denies execution unless explicitly authorized
• Block list (deny list) — allows execution except explicitly prohibited items
MONITORING & CONFIGURATION ENFORCEMENT
• Monitoring detects drift from hardened baseline (e.g., a disabled port reopened)
• Configuration Enforcement relies on:
• Standardized Configuration Baselines (NIST, CIS, org-defined)
• Automated Configuration Management Tools
• Continuous Monitoring & Compliance Checks
• Change Management processes
• Group Policy — Windows/AD centralized config management, linked to OUs (Organizational Units)
• SELinux — Linux kernel security module enforcing MAC (Mandatory Access Control); Android equivalent = SEAndroid
HARDENING TECHNIQUES
Physical Ports:
• Disable unnecessary USB/HDMI/serial ports
• Port control software (allow only approved devices)
• UEFI/BIOS password for boot-from-USB
• BadUSB — malicious firmware makes a USB device impersonate another class (e.g., keyboard/keylogger)
• O.MG cable — malicious USB-Lightning cable with built-in access point/keylogger
• Disable autorun for USB devices; use a sheep dip (sandboxed system) to test suspicious devices
Logical Ports: controlled via firewalls (port/IP/protocol filtering) and service hardening (updates, disabling unused services)
Encryption Techniques:
• FDE (BitLocker/FileVault)
• Removable Media Encryption
• VPN — secure tunnel against eavesdropping/on-path attacks
• Email Encryption — PGP, S/MIME
Host-Based Firewalls/IPS:
• Default-deny policy
• Traffic filtering by IP/protocol/service
• Integrates with SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)
INSTALLING ENDPOINT PROTECTION (DEPLOYMENT BEST PRACTICES)
• Create a Deployment Plan (order, timing, staging)
• Standardize Configurations
• Automate Deployments (SCCM, Group Policy)
• Apply Updates and Patches
• Monitor agents
• Centralize Management
CHANGING DEFAULTS & REMOVING UNNECESSARY SOFTWARE
• Change default passwords immediately (common vuln in multifunction printers, IoT)
• Remove unnecessary software/features to reduce attack surface
• Disable unneeded features (e.g., printer cloud printing, email, web server interfaces)
• Prefer encrypted protocols: HTTPS, SNMPv3
DECOMMISSIONING
• Data sanitization — securely erase/overwrite all data
• Factory reset device
• Physical destruction of storage (HDD/SSD/M.2) if sensitive data present
• Update inventory records / documentation
HARDENING SPECIALIZED DEVICES
• Applies to ICS (Industrial Control Systems), SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition), embedded systems, RTOS (Real-Time Operating Systems), IoT
• General controls: regular updates, disable unnecessary services, limit network access, secure credentials, RBAC
• Network-level: firewalls, IDS/IPS, TLS/SSH encryption, audits, pen tests
ICS/SCADA specific:
• Strict network segmentation
• Strong authentication/authorization
• Unidirectional gateways (data diodes) — data flows outward only, blocking inbound attacks
Embedded/RTOS specific:
• Security designed in from the start: secure coding, minimal design, secure boot, tamper-proofing
• Standards: Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408), IEC 62443, MISRA-C, CERT Secure Coding Standards
• Certifications: ISO 27001, IEC 61508

sections.title: Mobile Device Hardening
sections.content:
EXAM OBJECTIVE COVERED
• 4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources
SIMILARITIES/DIFFERENCES VS. TRADITIONAL ENDPOINTS
Similar: OS patches, strong passwords, endpoint protection, least privilege. Different: higher physical loss/theft risk → remote wipe, encryption, secure lock screens matter more. Also GPS/Bluetooth/NFC create extra attack surface.
DEPLOYMENT MODELS
Model | Description
BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) | Employee-owned; must meet org requirements; employee consents to audits/corporate app installs
COBO (Corporate Owned, Business Only) | Org-owned, business use only
COPE (Corporate Owned, Personally Enabled) | Org-owned/chosen, but allows personal use
CYOD (Choose Your Own Device) | Like COPE, but employee picks from a pre-approved device list
MOBILE DEVICE MANAGEMENT (MDM)
Centralized IT strategy to manage/secure/enforce policy on mobile endpoints.
• Maintains device inventory, authorized-device enforcement
• Enforces encryption, screen locks
• Remote lock/wipe
• Manages app allow/block lists, updates/patches, geofencing, geo-tracking
• Platforms: Apple MDM (built-in), Android Enterprise, and platform-agnostic tools like Microsoft Intune, VMware AirWatch, IBM MaaS360
FULL DEVICE ENCRYPTION
• iOS: all data always encrypted (key on device, used for wipe); "Data Protection" adds a second layer tied to user credential (email, some apps) — auto-enabled with passcode lock
• Android: no full-disk encryption as of Android 10 (performance cost); file-level encryption by default
• MicroSD HSM — small hardware security module for secure key storage, portable across devices
LOCATION SERVICES
• GPS (Global Positioning System) — satellite-based lat/long
• IPS (Indoor Positioning System) — triangulates via cell towers/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth
• A-GPS (Assisted GPS) — uses cell tower data to speed up positioning; can be jammed/spoofed
• Geofencing — virtual boundary triggering policy (e.g., reauthentication, disabling camera/mic)
• GPS tagging — geotag metadata embedded in media (privacy/OPSEC risk; e.g., Russian soldier selfie incident)
CONNECTION METHODS & RISKS
Cellular: bypasses enterprise network protections — mitigate via VPN, MDM, mobile threat defense, DLP, user training
Wi-Fi:
• Use WPA3 for corporate connections
• Risks: open/rogue APs, DNS spoofing
PAN (Personal Area Network):
• Ad hoc network — peer-to-peer, no fixed AP
• Wi-Fi Direct — one device acts as soft AP; relies on WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup, vulnerable)
• Tethering — sharing connection via USB/Bluetooth to one device
• Hotspot — sharing connection via Wi-Fi to multiple devices
• Should be disabled on enterprise networks (bypasses DLP/content filtering)
Bluetooth:
• Device Discovery — discoverable devices connect to any nearby Bluetooth device (even "hidden" devices can be detected)
• Bluejacking — unsolicited spam messages/vCards sent via Bluetooth
• Bluesnarfing — stealing data from a device by exploiting Bluetooth auth
• BlueBorne — Bluetooth exploit requiring no user interaction, no discovery needed
• Change default PINs (never "0000"); regularly audit pairing list
• BSC (Bluetooth Secure Connections, v4.0+) — improved resistance to eavesdropping/on-path attacks
• BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) Privacy — randomized addresses to prevent tracking
NFC (Near-Field Communication):
• Based on RFID; used for "bump" transactions, smart posters, mobile payments
• No native encryption — vulnerable to eavesdropping/on-path attacks
• Mobile wallets (Apple Pay, Google Pay, Samsung Pay) use one-time tokens, not raw card data
• Vulnerable to skimming (long card # + expiration) and RF flooding (DoS-like disruption)

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Establish configuration baselines per host type; monitor for compliance
• Configure full disk encryption
• Deploy endpoint protection covering antimalware, firewall, IDS, EDR, DLP
• Establish patch management/testing procedures for OS + third-party software
• Create a management plan for IoT devices
• For ICS/SCADA: secure procurement, cryptographic controls (auth/integrity/resiliency), access control/segmentation for OT networks, vendor patch support

practice_questions.q: Placing payment systems on a separate network segment from guest Wi-Fi is an example of:
practice_questions.explanation: Segmentation limits how far an attacker can move.

practice_questions.q: A documented set of approved, secure settings applied to every new server is called a:
practice_questions.explanation: Baselines define the secure starting configuration.

practice_questions.q: A firewall rule allows SSH from anywhere. The team changes it to allow SSH only from the admin subnet. What capability is being modified?
Which mitigation lets only approved applications run on a workstation?
options: Deny list of known malware only
practice_questions.explanation: An allow list blocks anything not explicitly approved.

practice_questions.q: Which wireless setup gives each user individual credentials checked against a RADIUS server?
practice_questions.explanation: Enterprise mode authenticates each user individually.

practice_questions.q: Which email security record lists the mail servers allowed to send mail for a domain?
practice_questions.explanation: Sender Policy Framework lists authorized senders.

practice_questions.q: Disabling unused services, closing unused ports and removing default accounts are all part of:
A company lets employees use personal phones for work but manages a separate work container on them. What deployment model is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Bring your own device uses personally owned phones.

practice_questions.q: Which email technology adds a digital signature to messages so receivers can verify they were not altered?
practice_questions.explanation: DomainKeys Identified Mail signs outgoing mail.

practice_questions.q: A retired server's drives are wiped and destroyed with a certificate of destruction. Which mitigation is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Proper decommissioning prevents data from leaking when assets are retired.
